Nondegree credentials may boost earnings, especially for those with just a high school diploma but sometimes even for those with college degrees.

About 37% of adults ages 25 to 64 with at least a high school diploma went on to earn nondegree credentials (NDC) — professional certifications, licenses or certificates — which typically target specific skills and occupations.

Full-time workers with NDCs often reported significantly higher median annual earnings than those without, regardless of educational attainment.

According to 2019–2024 combined data from the Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP) , full-time workers in this age group with an NDC reported 16.4% higher annual median earnings than those without one.

What Are Nondegree Credentials?

Earned outside of the traditional academic processes that lead to a college degree, NDCs are typically job-related and earned upon completion of a program of occupation-specific coursework, training or demonstration of specific skills.

The SIPP measures vocational and educational certificates, certifications and licenses of respondents age 18 and over.

Vocational and educational certificates , sometimes called diplomas, are earned from community, technical or career colleges as well as trade schools and universities. Most programs focus on job-skill development and career preparation. People with certificates enter a variety of fields from food service and maintenance to health care.

Certifications and licenses both require recipients to demonstrate job-specific knowledge, skills and abilities, which usually means passing an exam or other standardized assessment. Unlike certificates, certifications and licenses can expire.

Certifications are issued by industry-recognized boards, organizations and associations — the American Nursing Association, for example — and by private companies like Google. They are particularly common in healthcare and technical fields.

Licenses are legally necessary to work in an occupation and are issued by governmental agencies at the local, state or federal level. Each state and the District of Columbia have different rules, but all require emergency medical technicians, cosmetologists, barbers and attorneys to have a license.

Higher Pay With NDCs

Full-time workers with NDCs often reported significantly higher median annual earnings than those without, regardless of educational attainment (Figure 1).

Workers with certain types of NDCs who had completed high school or “some college” had median incomes on par with people with more education.

For instance, there was no difference in the median incomes of those who didn’t go beyond high school but had a certification or license and those who had some college or even an associate degree but no NDC.

Some college plus a certification or license was associated with higher median income than an associate degree alone.

Still, we can’t definitively credit NDCs for the increased earnings because the SIPP doesn’t ask when they were earned or whether they are relevant to respondents’ current jobs.

Bigger Payoff for Those With Lower Education Level

People with just a high school education were the only group to report significantly higher median earnings across all NDC types (Figure 2). They made 7.4% more with a certificate or certification/license, and about 21.0% more with a CCL, which is a combination of both.

Workers with some college or an associate degree plus a certification/license or combination CCL earned 10.9% to 16.2% more.

Only one type of NDC was connected with higher earnings for workers with bachelor’s degrees: those with a certification/license (alone and not in combination) earned about 5% more.

How Many Have NDCs?

Figure 3 illustrates the distribution and types of NDCs among full-time workers who had at least a high school diploma or equivalent but no more than a bachelor’s degree.

We excluded workers with advanced degrees because only 20.0% of the full-time working adult population has such specialized degrees.

We found that:

Roughly a third of working adults had some sort of NDC and certifications/licenses were the most common ones earned.

About 55% of NDC holders had only a certification/license and 23.5% a CCL.

Approximately 45% had a certificate, including 21.6% with a certificate alone and 23.5% in combination with a certification/license.

Who Had an NDC?

Figure 4 highlights the share of the full-time working population with an NDC by key demographic categories:

Women (36.1%) had NDCs at slightly higher rates than men (32.8%).

About 30% of Hispanic (28.9%) and Asian (30.3%) workers reported having NDCs (these two groups were not significantly different). By comparison, approximately a third of White (36.0%), Black (34.0%) and adults of another race or ethnicity (35.6%) earned NDCs.

NDCs were less common among workers ages 25 to 34 (29.3%) than among workers ages 35-64 (about 35%), suggesting that workers may seek more professional credentials later in their careers.

Roughly half of associate degree holders (46.7%) reported having an NDC, possibly because a high proportion (43.0%) of associate degrees of adults age 25 and older were occupational rather than academic , often preparing graduates for healthcare and other technical fields that demand highly specialized training and additional qualifications.

Which Occupations Had More Workers With NDCs?

To measure NDC attainment across jobs, we combined workers’ reported occupations into five categories based on the Current Population Survey’s Detailed Occupation Recodes (2018) :

Service . Healthcare support, food service, and custodial.

Sales/administrative. Sales roles and office and administrative support.

Farm/craft. Farming, fishing, forestry, construction and repair.

Production. Manufacturing and transportation.

Professional. Management, STEM (science, technology, engineering and mathematics), education, healthcare practitioner and legal.

Almost 40% of workers in service, farm/craft and professional occupations had at least one NDC (Figure 5).

This is not surprising given the extensive credentialing requirements for healthcare workers and information technology-related certifications for various software, programs and equipment. Farm and craft trades, like agriculture and plumbing, similarly require credentialing to work with hazardous chemicals, heavy machinery and complex systems.

NDCs were less common in production and sales/administrative occupations. Some, like retail, don’t require extensive technical training.

About the Data

Data are subject to nonsampling and sampling error. More information about SIPP sampling and accuracy can be found on our website.

Note: The figures in this story were revised September 24 based on updated weights in the Public-Use File. More information is available in the March 2026 User Note . While the revision to the weighting did result in some changes to the estimates, it did not change any of the conclusions made from statistical testing.

About 56% of U.S. workers said they have used Artificial Intelligence (AI) on the job for at least one of 11 tasks asked about on the U.S. Census Bureau’s March 2026 Household Trends and Outlook Pulse Survey (HTOPS).

The tasks covered a range of everyday work activities, such as searching for technical help, writing, generating ideas, and coding.

Those who reported using AI at work in the last week were asked how many additional hours they would’ve needed to finish their work without AI. A quarter said AI saved them less than an hour and 31% said AI saved them one to two hours.

The survey describes AI as the capability of computational systems to perform tasks typically associated with human intelligence, such as learning, reasoning, problem-solving, perception and decision-making.

The survey question provided examples of AI as machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, and voice recognition.

Among workers who used AI at work, about a third said it cut one or two hours from their tasks.

The HTOPS, a bi-monthly survey that provides timely insight on social and economic impacts on U.S. households, asked workers about their AI use for 11 job tasks. The top five ways people said they’ve used AI at work:

37% said to search for information or technical help.

32% to write communications, documentation or instructions.

32% to generate ideas.

31% to interpret, translate or summarize information.

27% to do administrative tasks.

Fewer U.S. workers reported using AI for other tasks like coding or modeling, customer support and managing logistics or supply chains.

How Often Workers Use AI and How Much Time They Save

About 24% of AI users at work — those who reported using AI for any of the survey’s 11 tasks – said they used AI every day in the last week.

Another 46% said they used it at least one day (but not every day), and 31% said they didn’t use it at all.

Those who reported using AI at work in the last week were asked how many additional hours they would’ve needed to finish their work without AI.

A quarter said AI saved them less than an hour and 31% said AI saved them one to two hours.

A smaller share (15%) reported AI cut their workload by three to four hours and another 15% said by more than four hours.

Some (10%) said AI didn’t save any time and 4% reported using AI required additional time to complete their work.

AI Use at Work by Educational Attainment

Higher shares of workers with a bachelor’s degree or higher reported using AI at work compared to those with lower levels of education.

For example, 46% of workers with a bachelor’s degree or higher reported using AI at work to interpret, translate or summarize information, compared with 25% of those with some college or an associate’s degree and 15% with a high school diploma or less (including high school equivalency).

Asked how often they used AI at work last week, 75% of those with a bachelor’s degree or higher said at least one day , compared with 62% with some college or an associate’s degree and 59% with a high school diploma/equivalency or less.

AI Use at Work by Sex

There were some differences in the tasks that men and women used AI for at work.

About 42% of male workers said they used it to search for information compared with 31% of female workers. And about a third of male workers (34%) used it to interpret, translate or summarize information compared to 28% of female workers.

When AI users at work were asked how much they used AI in the last week, 30% of male workers said they used it every day, compared with 17% of female workers. Half of female workers said they used it at least one day, but not every day, and 41% of male workers said the same.

About 3 in 10 male (28%) and female workers (32%) said they did not use AI last week.

AI Use at Work by Age

Younger workers were more likely to report using AI for four of the top five job tasks.

For example, 34% of workers ages 18 to 49 said they used it to write communications, documentation or instructions, compared with 29% of workers age 50 and older. There were no statistical differences in searching for information or technical help by age group.

About a quarter (25%) of AI users at work ages 18 to 49 and 20% of those age 50 and older reported using AI daily last week.

Additional Resources and Data

The HTOPS March 2026 table package also features findings on topics, such as employment, mental health and social connectedness.

The HTOPS March 2026 PUF contains data on the questions featured in this article and can be used to calculate standard errors for estimates presented here.

About the Research

All comparative statements have undergone statistical testing and, unless otherwise noted, all comparisons are statistically significant at the 90% confidence level.

All data are subject to error arising from a variety of sources, including sampling error, non-sampling error, modeling error, and any other sources of error. More information about the Household Trends and Outlook Pulse Survey is available here .

About 24% of AI users at work — those who reported using AI for any of the survey’s 11 tasks – said they used AI every day in the last week.

Smith. Johnson. Williams. Brown. Jones. Miller. Davis. Wilson.

These names were among the most common in the United States in 1790, when the first census was taken.

Little has changed 230 years later. Despite a more than 84-fold increase in the population, those same names remained among the top 15 in the most recent 2020 Census.

The U.S. Census Bureau today released the 2020 Names Data , which tallies rankings of the nation’s most popular monikers and how many people share each one.

Last names tend to cluster by racial and Hispanic origin group, and each group experiences a different amount of clustering.

And for the first time since 1990, the tables also list the most popular first names by race and Hispanic origin and by sex — showing less variety among the most popular men’s first names than women’s names.

As a result, eight of the top 10 most-used first names in the United States were traditionally male.

The data release is a tally of all the first names reported in the 2020 Census and a separate tally of the last names. It is not a release of the full legal names of census respondents.

The term “predominantly” is used where the majority of people using certain names identified with a single Race, Hispanic origin, or Sex category. For example, “Garcia” is a predominantly Hispanic last name because 91% of the people named Garcia chose Hispanic in their response to the 2020 Census.

Leading Last Names

The top five last names (Smith, Johnson, Williams, Brown and Jones) were the same for three decades — 2000, 2010 and 2020 — and among the top 15 in 1790 (Figure 1).

“It is certainly surprising given the enormous change in population since then … and the immigration in that period from all around the world,” said Joshua Comenetz, senior geographer at the Census Bureau and manager of the Census Names Project.

The rise in predominantly Hispanic last names between 2000 and 2020 is also notable.

In 2000, the top 50 last names included 10 that were used at least 90% of the time by respondents who identified as Hispanic. Garcia, the top-ranked among them in 8th place in 2000, jumped to 6th in 2010.

In the 2020 count, the rankings had largely stabilized. All the top 15 last names held their place except for Rodriguez, which bumped up into 8th place, moving Davis down a notch.

Name Concentration

For example, people of Hispanic or Latino origin have the highest percentage of their population (14.2%) sharing the group’s top 10 last names (Table 1).

In other words, fewer names cover a larger swath of the Hispanic or Latino population compared to other groups.

“I’m not surprised there,” Comenetz says, “because the most common predominantly Hispanic names have one language origin.”

In contrast, respondents who identified as White alone (i.e., White and no other race or origin) had the smallest percentage of their population (4.4%) using the top 10 last names for their racial group.

In short, a greater number of last names was needed to cover 25% of the White alone population compared to the other groups.

Differences in concentration may influence which names climb the ranks.

Fastest Growing

All but one of the fastest-growing last names among the top 1,000 were predominantly Asian between 2010 and 2020 (Table 2).

This reflects a shift in immigration patterns. The 2000 to 2010 list of fastest growing names included several predominantly Hispanic names.

“Among the fastest growing names list, they’re all predominantly Asian, except the name Ali,” said Comenetz. “It’s common in South Asia, East Africa and the Middle East.”

Greater Variety for Women

First name data are available for the first time since 1990.

Despite women outnumbering men in the United States, the top five first names among the 2020 U.S. population were traditionally male: Michael, John, James, David and Robert.

Why? Because a larger fraction of men share the most common male names, while a smaller fraction of women share the most common female names.

“Sixteen percent of men have the top 10 male names,” said Comenetz. “For women, it’s only a little under 8%.”

In other words, women had more first name variety than men.

Compared to men, nearly three times as many names were needed to cover 25% of the female population (Table 3).

This is reflected in the overall first name ranking, where eight of the top 10 most common first names are predominantly male (Table 4).

Comparing Name Datasets

How popular is your name for newborns? You can find out by looking at the annual Social Security Administration (SSA) release of babies’ first names, with data going back to the 1800s.

Comparing the 2020 first name datasets from SSA and the Census Bureau, there is little overlap between the two lists (Table 5). The SSA counts the names of the babies born in 2020, while the Census Bureau counts the names of all respondents.

This comparison shows that there is not much overlap in the popularity of names of babies born in 2020 and the names of the total U.S. population that year.

“The census represents a kind of average of everybody currently living here,” says Comenetz. “There’s so much variety in how people name their kids that a single year does not fit the average.”

Sharing a Name

Most first names are used 95% or more of the time by either men or women exclusively but there are a few that are equally common among both.

Some in the top 1,000 first names are close to a 50/50 split between the sexes (Table 6).

Popular first names may come and go, but it’s clear the most common last names have staying power.

“Despite all the changes in population, I suspect Smith would still be the most popular last name in 2075,” said Comenetz. “I’d be surprised if it isn’t.”

Travis Shoemaker is a writer/editor at the Census Bureau.

More than nine out of 10 U.S. households have air conditioning (AC) in their homes, but that national count is meaningless to communities where AC access is virtually nonexistent.

As the scorching days of summer approach, state and local governments want to know which neighborhoods are most vulnerable to heat risk.

The U.S. Census Bureau recently released the Local Air Conditioning Estimates (LACE) , an experimental measure of air conditioning prevalence at the state, county and tract levels. These estimates can help community planners gauge who is most at risk of heat exposure and compare air conditioning access across communities, states and regions.

Getting data down to the neighborhood level is even more compelling as it can help state and local governments prepare for extreme heat events.

Municipalities that try to address extreme heat dangers often lack consistent local estimates of households that have air conditioning. Some areas produce their own estimates, but those don’t allow for wider comparisons like LACE.

How LACE Can Help

Viewing AC access at different levels of geography tells a more complete story.

For example, statewide data show low access in some states in the West, Great Lakes and Northeast (Figure 1). But once you drill down to the counties in those states, it’s clear that each has pockets of high, medium and low air conditioning access (Figure 2).

For example, some cities offer portable air conditioning units to residents who don’t have air conditioning in their home. Knowing which neighborhoods have the greatest need helps target community outreach and distribution plans.

Take Salt Lake County, Utah (Figure 3). Only 6.6% of households countywide don’t have air conditioning, according to LACE. But estimates range between 0.0% and 23.2% at the neighborhood and tract levels.

LACE helps municipalities identify areas with households that likely lack air conditioning. Having this data as part of the experimental data product series allows local governments to contact the Census Bureau and provide feedback on the accuracy and utility of these estimates.

About LACE

The Census Bureau produces LACE data based on responses to the American Housing Survey (AHS) and the American Community Survey (ACS) .

The AHS asks questions about air conditioning the ACS doesn’t and publishes estimates for the nation, census divisions and select metro areas. The ACS has a larger sample size, allowing us to publish granular estimates for smaller geographies.

By using machine learning and cross-survey modeling, we combine the strengths of both surveys to provide estimates of air conditioning prevalence down to the tract level.

Cross-survey modeling is a new technique that uses data from one survey to create an algorithm that is then applied to determine how respondents may have answered the same question on a different survey.

This involves taking one survey or dataset with detailed subject matter and applying the characteristics to a dataset with detailed geographic information — in this case, the AHS and ACS.

The result: experimental estimates of air conditioning prevalence for smaller geographies.

LACE was recently featured in a webinar to help data users learn about the techniques used to create the estimates in more detail and showcase ways to use them.

The Census Bureau welcomes feedback on the quality of the LACE estimates, opinions on the quality of the techniques and information on the usefulness of the data. Feedback can be sent to [email protected] .

Chase Sawyer is a technical lead for modeled data product development at the Census Bureau.

The number of women who were unmarried when they gave birth in the last year dropped to about 1.2 million in 2023, around a 15% decline in just over a decade, according to a recent U.S. Census Bureau report .

Almost one-third (30.9%) of the 4 million women ages 15 to 50 who gave birth in the last year in 2023 were unmarried. In 2011, 35.7% or 1.5 million of the 4.1 million in that age group who gave birth in the last year were unmarried.

Some of the differences in geographic patterns may be related to socioeconomic characteristics like poverty and income , which vary by state and county.

The national decline in unmarried women having babies is mirrored in most states. In states where the numbers did not drop, the numbers remained statistically unchanged.

Variation by State in 2023

Eight states in the South — Alabama, Florida, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, South Carolina, Texas and West Virginia — had higher levels of recent births to unmarried women than the nation.

In contrast, six states in the Midwest (Iowa, Kansas, Minnesota, North Dakota, South Dakota, Wisconsin), four in the Northeast (New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, Vermont), and four in the West (Colorado, Idaho, Utah, Washington) had lower levels of recent births to unmarried women than the nation. Just one state in the South (Virginia) had lower than national levels of recent births to unmarried women.

Variation by Metropolitan Statistical Area in 2023

The picture is more complex at the metropolitan statistical area (MSA) level.

MSAs with higher-than-average percentages of unmarried women who gave birth in the last year were in the South, parts of the Midwest, California and Puerto Rico.

Brunswick-St. Simons, Georgia had among the highest percentage: 70.7%.

MSAs with a lower-than-average percentage were scattered throughout the United States, but had higher concentrations in the Northeast, parts of the Midwest and the West.

Pocatello, Idaho had among the lowest percentage of women with a recent birth who were unmarried: 6.2%.

Socioeconomic Context

The report shows a strong positive correlation at the state level between the percentage of women with a recent birth who were unmarried and the percentage of people in households below the poverty line.

Marriage Rates

Varying state marriage rates are another factor. For example, Washington, D.C., Colorado and Nebraska had among the nation’s highest marriage rates in 2022 while New Mexico and Puerto Rico had among the lowest.

It is worth noting that several of the MSAs that had among the lowest percentages of women with a recent birth who were unmarried are home to large state universities: Amherst Town-Northampton, MA (University of Massachusetts Amherst); Logan, UT-ID (Utah State University); Provo-Orem-Lehigh, UT (Utah Valley University); Ames, IA (Iowa State University); and Lawrence, KS (University of Kansas).

This aligns with previous research that has found that women with higher education (a bachelor’s degree or higher) or who are economically advantaged are more likely to be married .

Recent Census Bureau research shows that women with a first birth between 2020 to 2024 with a bachelor’s degree were more likely to be married than those without a degree.

The U.S. percentage differs between the state and MSA tables and figures because the state data come from the 2023 American Community Survey 1-year estimates and the MSA data come from the 2023 American Community Survey 5-year estimates. This page provides guidance and information on differences between the two files.

Lydia Anderson is a statistician at the Census Bureau.

The summer road trip is classic Americana. Every year, sightseers cross the country to visit amusement parks, museums, restaurants, gift shops, hotels and more.

Here we provide you with an economic travelogue to four tourist hotspots: California, Florida, Nevada and Washington, D.C.

We begin our journey with a new infographic that highlights the revenue estimates from recreation-related industries in these destinations, according to the 2022 Economic Census and Census of Governments data, the most recent stats available.

Washington, D.C.

The start of your virtual vacation is in the nation’s capital, Washington, D.C.

You could visit one of the many Museums in the district, which brought in a total of $177.3 million in revenue in 2022.

When you’re done perusing the exhibits, you might explore one of the nearby state and local parks and recreation areas. D.C.’s state and local parks generated $24.9 million in revenue in 2022.

Next, you head south to Florida for a visit to one of the Sunshine State’s many Amusement and Theme Parks , which brought in $7.8 billion in revenues in 2022 (Figure 2).

Upon your exit, you’ll likely walk through a Gift, Novelty, and Souvenir Retailer . These shops generated $1.9 billion in revenue for Florida in 2022.

You hit the road again, leaving the waters of Florida for the high desert of Nevada.

Feeling lucky, you visit one of the Silver State’s many Casino Hotels , which in 2022 made $27.3 billion in revenue (Figure 3).

Gambling is hungry work, so you grab a bite at one of the nearby Restaurants and Other Eating Places . These establishments generated $10.2 billion in revenue for Nevada in 2022.

California

The road trip is nearly over. Before you head home, you decide to go all the way to the Pacific Ocean with a visit to California.

You tour some of the Motion Picture and Video Production studios that generated $59.0 billion in revenue in 2022 for the state.

The next day, you leave the studio backlots and head up to California’s Wine Country for a tasting or two to toast your journey’s end. California Wineries brought in $19.3 billion in revenue in 2022.

captures.text:
As the United States hosts the 2026 International Federation of Association Football (FIFA) World Cup along with Canada and Mexico this month, soccer teams from around the world are likely to draw support from foreign-born fans in the United States.

The global tournament brings people from six continents to the United States, a nation shaped and developed by people from across the world. In the 2020 to 2024 ACS, 47.3 million foreign-born people called the U.S. home.

The foreign-born population is not evenly spread across the United States, with some global communities heavily concentrated in just a few states.

The World Cup offers a unique opportunity to examine how people from participating nations are represented across the country and where they live.

Among countries competing this summer, many have relatively small populations in the United States that are not large enough to be analyzed in detail. We focus on the 10 countries with the largest foreign-born U.S. populations and show how they are distributed across U.S. host cities.

One Clear Leader

No other country comes close to Mexico’s numbers, which stand far above the rest with nearly 11 million people in the United States born there. The next largest foreign-born populations in the United States with about 1 million or less are Korea and Colombia.

The rest of the top 10 list includes countries from many world regions.

Many Roads, Few Destinations

California, the nation’s most populous state, is home to the largest state shares of several foreign-born populations, including those from Canada, Germany, Iran, Japan, Korea, and Mexico.

Florida also stands out, especially for its high numbers of people born in Colombia, Haiti, and Brazil.

The concentration is particularly striking among some populations: more than half of the Iranian-born population in the United States lives in California, and nearly half of the Haitian-born population lives in Florida.

U.S. Host Cities From Miami to Kansas City

Foreign-born population shares vary widely across the 11 U.S. metro areas hosting World Cup matches.

In Miami and the San Francisco Bay Area (San Jose-Sunnyvale-Santa Clara metro area), over 40% of residents are foreign-born, compared with about 7.3% in the Kansas City metro area.

These differences reflect longstanding migration and settlement patterns across the United States.

On the East Coast, a Different Mix

In several East Coast host cities, no single country of birth accounts for a large share of the foreign-born population. Even so, a few groups still stand out:

In the Miami metro area, the Haitian-born population accounts for about 8.8% of the foreign-born.

The Ecuadorian-born population accounted for about 4.8% of the foreign-born population in the New York/ New Jersey metro area.

Among Boston’s foreign-born population, 7.9% are from Brazil.

In the remaining U.S. host cities, including the Atlanta, Dallas, and Houston metro areas, Mexico is the top country of birth among the foreign-born population.

The World Cup brings people from many countries together on the field and in the stands.

Interested in learning more? Visit the Foreign-Born Population page for additional information and resources.

Lauren Medina is a demographic research manager at the Census Bureau.

Shabnam Shenasi Azari and Komba Gbondo-Tugbawa are statisticians at the Census Bureau.

captures.date_review_note: Official source page/API publication verified; earlier publication or repost elsewhere remains to be checked. Do not equate an URL stamp or update with first publication.

captures.text:
Last year was one of the nation’s most active tornado seasons on record, with approximately 1,559 tornadoes — 27% higher than the 30-year average from 1991–2020, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration .

The number of tornadoes not only grew but shifted eastward during that period: tornado activity decreased in the west by 25% and increased in the east by 12% (Figure 1). This shift is especially concerning because tornadoes are now increasingly affecting southern states with a large concentration of mobile home communities.

The National Weather Service reports that mobile home residents are 15 to 20 times more likely to be killed in a tornado than those living in site‑built housing.

To help identify where these communities are located and who may be most vulnerable to tornadoes, communities can turn to Census Bureau data.

The American Community Survey ( ACS ) publishes data that enable communities to gauge risk to residents. The ACS contains variables on community vulnerability, including housing characteristics. This provides a national framework to identify tornado risk and prepare people for disaster.

The Community Resilience Estimates ( CRE ), built with ACS data and small area modeling techniques, also help identify populations that may have difficulty with disaster recovery.

Community leaders, emergency managers and everyday citizens can use Census Bureau data, like the ACS and the CRE, to better understand the disaster vulnerability of any neighborhood in the nation.

Seasonal Change

Tornado activity isn’t only shifting eastward — it’s also breaking out of the traditional late-spring-into-summer season, now stretching into winter and early spring.

Between 1950 and 2009, tornado activity was strongly concentrated in the spring months, when nearly two‑thirds of all tornadoes occurred between April and June.

From 2010 to 2025, tornado activity expanded, with higher tornado counts in January through April, and notable increases in October and December (Figure 2).

Summertime tornado activity dropped compared to 1950-2009. The tornado season now begins earlier, ramps up more gradually, and extends later into the year.

This growing threat of near year-round tornadoes is most pronounced in the South, particularly the Gulf Coast states of Alabama, Louisiana and Mississippi, where moisture-rich air creates an uninterrupted, seven-month tornado season in the cooler months.

Communities at Risk

In addition to increasing tornado activity, Alabama, Louisiana and Mississippi have some of the nation’s highest concentrations of mobile homes, also referred to as manufactured housing (Figure 3 and 4).

“Site-built structures” constructed directly in the ground offer protection against weaker tornadoes. But manufactured housing can be severely damaged or destroyed by even the lowest-rated tornado on the Enhanced Fujita (EF) Scale, which classifies tornadoes by severity of damage caused.

To gauge tornado risk in Alabama, Louisiana, and Mississippi, we selected one representative community in each state. Using ACS and CRE data, the analysis provides an overview of each community’s vulnerability through a socioeconomic profile paired with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s count of tornado activity.

The CRE’s measure of vulnerability includes ten components from poverty and disability to health insurance coverage and vehicle access. Individuals with three or more components are considered vulnerable to the impacts of a natural disaster.

Greene County had the largest tornado‑rate increase among the three example communities. It is Alabama’s 2nd most vulnerable county according to the CRE measures of population vulnerability.

Other underlying socioeconomic factors mean that even weak tornadoes can have a disproportionate impact on the county:

Increase in tornado events, 2010-2025: An unprecedented 171% jump.

CRE vulnerable population estimate: 38.9%

Housing stock: 34.7% manufactured homes.

Poverty rate: 33%.

Disability rate: Over 18%.

One quarter of residents are 65 or older.

Low labor force participation.

As Louisiana’s third most vulnerable parish, according to the CRE, St. Helena Parish’s housing stock is 45% mobile homes. The parish experienced a sizable increase in tornado events, and its other socioeconomic characteristics amplify the consequences of weak and moderate tornadoes:

Increase in tornado events, 2010-2025: 67%.

CRE vulnerable population estimate: 36.1%

Poverty rate: over 32%.

Disability rate: 27%.

About one-quarter of residents are age 65 or older.

Mississippi has a higher number of tornado events compared to Alabama or Louisiana.

While Scott County ranked 50th in vulnerability out of Mississippi’s 82 counties, it has a higher percentage of residents with three or more CRE vulnerability components than about 83% of all U.S. counties. More than a third of its housing is mobile homes (35.8%).

The county faces meaningful risk, but measured against the examples in Louisiana and Alabama, it has more resources due to lower poverty and a healthier labor market:

Increase in tornado events, 2010-2025: 12%.

CRE vulnerable population estimate: 27.9%

Poverty rate: 22.2%, lower than in the other two chosen counties.

Median household income supports a broader labor market and more diverse local economy, by comparison.

Tornado Cost & Safety

In addition to the toll tornadoes take on people, they are among the costliest weather hazards in the United States. Since 1980, tornadoes have accounted for nearly half of all billion-dollar weather disasters, and annual losses have increased by more than $1 billion over the past two decades.

What can be done? The first line of defense is accurate detection and warning systems, which are essential as tornado risks evolve across regions and seasons.

Assisted by census data, decision makers, emergency planners and ordinary residents can strengthen their tornado-prone community’s ability to adapt as tornado activity shifts eastward and extends later into the year.

Census Bureau data offer communities a place to start by identifying where vulnerable communities are located, including areas with a higher percentage of mobile homes. The data help leaders focus planning, improve outreach and support the people who need it most.

Janie Forbes is a geographer at the Census Bureau.

Chase Sawyer, a demographic statistician at the Census Bureau, contributed to this story.

captures.text:
U.S. real median household income was $87,460 in 2025, up 2.6% from the previous year and the highest on record since 1967 when the U.S. Census Bureau began tracking this measure, according to a new report released today.

Median household income is the midpoint where half of households have higher income, and half have lower income. All estimates here are adjusted for inflation.

Historic High

The median household income estimate of $85,210 for 2024 was not statistically different from the estimate in 2019, the last year prior to the COVID-19 pandemic and the record high to that point.

At the top of the income distribution, this was the third consecutive year-over-year increase in both pre- and post-tax income at the 90th percentile.

According to the Census Bureau’s Income in the United States: 2025 , the median household income in 2025 of $87,460 (±$1,040) was higher than in both 2019 and 2024 (Figure 1).

Post-Tax Income

The Census Bureau also produces income estimates after accounting for taxes and credits .

Post-tax median household income was $76,060 (±$712) in 2025, up 3.1% from $73,760 in 2024 but not a record high.

The nation turns 250 this year and Americans’ median age — the age at which half of the population is younger and half is older — continues to rise, climbing from 39.2 in 2024 to 39.4 in 2025.

We use population estimates released today to examine changes in the U.S. age structure by sex from 2001, when the median age was 35.6, to 2025.

One striking shift is that while women continued to outnumber men at older ages, the gap between the sexes narrowed in the past 25 years (Figure 1).

"Mortality rates for older men have been decreasing faster than for women and, as a result, men's share of the older population has increased."

— Marc Perry, senior demographer in the U.S. Census Bureau’s Population Division

In 2001, there were 70.6 males for every 100 females age 65 and older. By 2025, the ratio had increased substantially to 81.6.

The gap among those age 80 and older narrowed even more dramatically — from 50.9 males per 100 females in 2001 to 68.3 in 2025.

"Mortality rates for older men have been decreasing faster than for women and, as a result, men's share of the older population has increased," said Marc Perry, senior demographer in the U.S. Census Bureau’s Population Division. "But the mortality gap between men and women is still there. In fact, the current mortality rate for men age 65 and older is roughly where the equivalent rate for women was 50 years ago."

According to the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS), the age-adjusted death rate for males age 65 and older was 8,285.0 per 100,000 people in 1970. By 2022, it had dropped to 5,205.7, a decline of 3,079 deaths per 100,000.

Female mortality also dropped, but not as rapidly. The death rate for females age 65 and older was 5,621.3 per 100,000 people in 1970 and 3,918.7 in 2022, a decline of 1,703 deaths per 100,000.

The Tales Population Pyramids Can Tell

Figure 2 shows the U.S. population pyramid for 2025, with males on the left (blue) and females on the right (orange).

In 2025, the population pyramid shows clear bumps in certain age ranges like 61 to 79. People in this group — which includes those born between 1946 and 1964 during the post-World War II fertility surge — are often referred to as baby boomers.

Despite its size, the distinct visibility of the baby boomers as a group has diminished as they age and their mortality increases. Their prominence has also been diluted by the growth in younger age groups, largely due to immigration.

The shift is vivid when we animate the population pyramid from 2001 to 2025 (Figure 3).

Another notable change is the impact of declining fertility, apparent in the narrowing of the bars at the youngest ages as we move forward in time.

In 2001, the total fertility rate (TFR) was 2.11 births per woman, according to the NCHS. By 2024, the fertility rate had dropped to 1.63 births per woman. At the peak of the baby boom in 1957, the TFR was more than double at 3.77 .

“With the persistently low fertility rates in recent years and baby boomers experiencing higher mortality, the age structure of the U.S. population has morphed over time,” Perry said. “These trends have also contributed to the slowdown in national growth in recent years.”

History and the Gap Among Older Males and Females

Why women outnumber men at older ages has been attributed to a combination of behavioral, lifestyle and biological factors. Another explanation is generational history.

In 2001, the Greatest Generation was between 74 and 100 years old. Closely tied to World War II, its members were between 18 and 44 when the war ended in 1945. This generation’s sex disparity — fewer men than women — reflects, in part, the heavy toll of male lives lost during the war decades earlier.

As that generation grew older, the gap gradually narrowed as cohorts whose mortality was less affected by war entered those age groups.

Future Implications

As the population ages and the traditional longevity gap between men and women narrows, there could be some potential social impacts, including:

Health care. An aging population could put a strain on skilled nursing facilities and health care workers.

Dependency ratio. The U.S. dependency ratio may also increase , which could place additional pressures on the working-age population to support health care, social services, education and other institutions.

Later marriages. As people live longer, they have more time to divorce or (re)marry at older ages . The decreasing disparity in the number of older men and women could create a more balanced pool of eligible partners at later ages.

Extended families. If men continue to see improvements in old-age mortality rates, people could have more time to spend with their aging parents and grandparents — especially fathers and grandfathers.

Like the baby boom, sudden demographic shifts are possible and could alter the trajectory of the age structure of the United States over the next 25 years.

Upcoming releases of the Census Bureau’s population estimates will help us monitor future population changes.

In May, new subcounty estimates will reveal how cities and towns have changed in the last year. In June, the Census Bureau is set to release age, sex, race, and Hispanic origin estimates for the nation, states, counties, and metropolitan and micropolitan statistical areas.

Luke T. Rogers is a senior research scientist and demographer at the Census Bureau.

The smallest possible businesses, nonemployer establishments (those with no paid employees), accounted for 78.4% of all U.S. establishments in 2023, and brought in nearly $1.8 trillion in revenue that year — proof of the power of small business in America’s economy.

The Small Business Administration (SBA) defines a small business as an independent business with fewer than 500 employees and has celebrated Small Business Week every May since 1963 to recognize U.S. entrepreneurs and small business owners.

The U.S. Census Bureau plays a part too, tracking key data points and resources to provide a rich profile of the nation’s small businesses.

There were 5.58 million U.S. firms that had at least one employee but fewer than 500 employees in 2023, up from 5.53 million in 2022.

The SBA is set to host events across the country during Small Business Week – May 3 to May 9, 2026 – including a free virtual summit for aspiring entrepreneurs and small business owners, and in-person sessions on a variety of business topics. Additionally, a recently recorded Census webinar on Creating a Data-Driven Business Plan is available on demand here .

The Nation’s Small Business Landscape

The Census Bureau publishes a variety of data and resources about the nation’s small businesses.

There were 5.58 million U.S. firms that had at least one employee but fewer than 500 employees in 2023, up from 5.53 million in 2022, according to the annual Business Dynamics Statistics (Figure 1).

An establishment is a single physical location of a business. A firm is a business organization consisting of one or more establishments under the same owner.

In addition to these small employer businesses (those with at least one paid employee), there are many self-employed U.S. entrepreneurs who run nonemployer businesses.

In 2023, there were 30,427,808 nonemployer establishments, up from 29,811,495 in 2022 – and they brought in nearly $1.8 trillion (6.4% of the Gross Domestic Product or GDP in 2023) in total revenue, according to Nonemployer Statistics (NES).

Nonemployer businesses operate in all sectors of the economy like retail, manufacturing and services.

Women-Owned Employer Businesses

The number of employer businesses owned by women jumped nearly 20% (from 1,134,549 to 1,356,990) between 2017 and 2023, according to the 2024 Annual Business Survey (ABS), which reported 2023 data.

Of those businesses, the number owned by veterans and minorities also went up. Between 2017 and 2023 (Note: Minority-owned firms are classified as any race and ethnicity combination other than non-Hispanic and White):

The number of female veteran-owned employer firms grew 25.7%.

The number of minority women-owned employer firms grew 49.8%.

Measuring the Pulse of U.S. Businesses

The Census Bureau’s Business Trends and Outlook Survey (BTOS) publishes data every two weeks, helping measure the “pulse” of the U.S. economy.

The BTOS covers current performance, changes in revenue, employment, hours worked, demand and prices from U.S. employer businesses.

It provides local, state and federal officials near real-time, nationally representative data for policy and decision-making, including after natural disasters or during economic crises. It also provides insights into recovery after these events.

BTOS data products were designed to allow users to understand business trends across the economy. Data is provided by employment class sizes with granular breakouts of firms ranging from one to four employees to those with less than 500 employees.

How to Start or Expand Your Small Business

Interested in starting a small business?

Use the Census Bureau webpage to find data tools and free training opportunities. Among them:

Small Business resource page . Helps businesses identify their customer needs and tap into new markets.

Census Business Builder (CBB) . A suite of services to help entrepreneurs examine competitors and the best location(s) to start their businesses. Small businesses can use the CBB to craft their own business plans.

Data User Guidance: Purposes and Uses of Economic Census Statistics . Provides key examples of how small businesses can use census data and tools for business planning.

Webinars . The Census Bureau hosts a variety of talks on business-related subjects, like last year’s webinar on Building a Better Business Plan Using Free Census Data .

Adam Grundy is a supervisory statistician at the Census Bureau.

The nation’s fertility rate has dropped nearly every year since 2007 , but this national decline masks substantial geographic variation.

Fertility rates differ widely across U.S. counties, and even within individual states there are often both high and low fertility counties.

By combining population estimates data released today on the age characteristics of U.S. counties with birth data released in March , we calculated the general fertility rate (GFR) for every county in the nation.

Counties with the most births are often not the ones with the highest fertility rates.

The GFR is the number of births per 1,000 females ages 15 to 44, and this story focuses only on U.S. counties that had at least 1,000 females in that age group in 2025 (2,703 of the 3,144 counties).

National Fertility Decline With Regional Variations

Nationally, the GFR has dropped from 69.5 in 2007 to 53.1 in 2025 — the lowest level reported in the national data series , which is available back to 1909.

Although there is no direct comparison of general fertility rates to total fertility rates (TFR), they go hand in hand.

In 2007, the national GFR was just below 70 (69.5) when total fertility rates were about 2.1 births per woman, which is generally considered “ replacement level .” In 2024, the GFR was 53.8 and the TFR was 1.6 .

In line with the nation, all regions were well below the 70 GFR threshold in 2025.

The South had the highest GFR at 55.8, followed closely by the Midwest at 54.7. The West had a GFR of 51.0, and the Northeast came in lowest, at 49.9.

Even with low GFRs, all regions experienced more births than deaths between 2024 and 2025. That’s because it takes time for low fertility rates to alter the population age structure, and even then, other demographic factors like migration and mortality affect the balance of births and deaths.

Where Are County Fertility Rates Highest?

There are clusters of high GFR counties in many, but not all, states.

For example, there are high GFR counties in southeastern North Carolina that extend into South Carolina, and in southern Georgia that extend into northern Florida.

Moving westward, many states have at least one cluster of counties with high GFRs.

Figure 1 shows the GFR values for counties in the United States in 2025.

Notably, there are only a few states that do not have any counties with a GFR above 60, including the entirety of New England: Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Vermont.

High Numbers of Births Do Not Always Equal High Fertility

The next part of our analysis examined fertility rates and births by county type: metro, micro and counties outside metro and micro areas . This is presented as a scatterplot in Figure 2, which also scales the dots for each county by population size of females ages 15 to 44.

One key pattern emerges from the graphic right away: counties with the most births are often not the ones with the highest fertility rates. In fact, the data suggest the opposite: counties with the highest numbers of births frequently have fertility rates below the median of all counties.

More populated counties tend to have more births because of their sheer size, but fertility rates can be impacted by a variety of factors: from the age structure of the population to other social or economic conditions.

The blue dots in Figure 2 (metro counties) often have thousands — or tens of thousands — of births, but many are clearly below the median county fertility rate of 59.1.

For example, Los Angeles County — the nation’s most populous — had the most births by far in 2025 (over 91,000), but a GFR of only 44.1.

Counties with both higher births and higher fertility rates were uncommon among large U.S. counties, but there were a few standouts in Texas. Among all counties with at least 20,000 births in 2025, the highest three general fertility rates were all in Texas:

Dallas County: 37,108 births, GFR of 62.6.

Harris County: 65,753 births, GFR of 59.2.

Tarrant County: 27,795 births, GFR of 57.0.

Fertility rates differ widely across U.S. counties, and even within individual states there are often both high and low fertility counties.

By combining population estimates data released today on the age characteristics of U.S. counties with birth data released in March , we calculated the general fertility rate (GFR) for every county in the nation.
Counties with the most births are often not the ones with the highest fertility rates.
The GFR is the number of births per 1,000 females ages 15 to 44, and this story focuses only on U.S. counties that had at least 1,000 females in that age group in 2025 (2,703 of the 3,144 counties).

Nationally, the GFR has dropped from 69.5 in 2007 to 53.1 in 2025 — the lowest level reported in the national data series , which is available back to 1909.

The world is getting older, faster than ever before. So is the United States, whose share of population age 65 and over is projected to jump from 18.9% in 2025 to 23.4% by 2060, according to a new U.S. Census Bureau report.

An Aging World: 2025 shows that despite continued growth of its older population, the nation will still be younger than nearly half the world’s countries by 2060.

In 160 countries — mostly in Africa, Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean — the population age 85 and over is expected to quadruple between 2025 and 2060.

“In 2025, the United States ranked as the 48th oldest country out of 227,” said Maria Aysa Lastra, a senior demographer at the Census Bureau. “By 2060, the country will fall to 110th place because countries in other regions are aging much more rapidly.”

By 2025, for the first time in human history, the share of adults age 65 and over outnumbered the share of children ages 0 to 5 in the world’s population – a gap projected to increase in the coming years.

How the World Is Aging

In 2025, Japan was the oldest country in the world with 29.7% of its population age 65 and over. By 2060, however, projected global aging will have accelerated so much that a share that size won’t even be among the top 25 oldest.

That year, Japan is expected to drop down to the third oldest country, with South Korea taking the lead with 41% of its population age 65 and over (Figure 1).

Europe is projected to remain the world’s “oldest” region, with the percent of its population age 65 and over increasing from 21.0% to 30.8% between 2025 and 2060.

By 2060, however, we project that in sheer numbers, there will be more people in that age group in Africa (249 million) than in Europe (214 million).

Older Adults Are Driving Most of the World’s Population Growth

The world population passed 8 billion in 2023 and is expected to grow by more than 2 billion by 2060. More than half that growth — about 1.148 billion people — will likely come from increases in the population age 65 and over.

The share of the world population age 65 and over is projected to nearly double, from 10.5% in 2025 to 19.6% by 2060.

In 160 countries — mostly in Africa, Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean — the population age 85 and over is expected to quadruple between 2025 and 2060 (Figure 2).

Many of the largest cohorts ever born are in places where liv­ing beyond 85 was once rare but is becoming commonplace.

Historic Shift: More Older Adults Than Young Children

Until very recently, children ages 0 to 5 made up a larger share of the world population than adults age 65 and over. That changed between 2020 and 2025, when the share of older adults eclipsed this youngest group for the first time (Figure 3).

Another expectation: the share of women will continue to be greater than that of men, thanks to women’s longer life expectancy. But this gap is expected to narrow from 80.6 males for every 100 females age 65 and over in 2025, to 84.7 males for every 100 females in 2060.

Living Longer — But Not Always Healthier

People are living longer but the number of years they spend in good health has not risen at the same rate, a challenge for all aging nations.

In the United States, for example, the proportion of years lived in full health after age 60 decreased by more than 2 percentage points between 2000 and 2019 – slightly more for men than for women.

Between 2016 and 2019, 73% of U.S. adults age 65 and over lived with two or more chronic illnesses.

Older adults had more mobility issues than younger populations in all countries. But mobility problems in the United States seemed to start at earlier ages (Figure 4). In 2018, around 60% of adults ages 60 to 69 in the United States and China reported mobility problems, compared to less than 30% that age in Switzerland.

COVID 19 and Dementia Among Top 5 Leading Causes of Death in 2021

According to the report, COVID-19 and Alzheimer’s disease and other dementias were among the top 5 leading causes of death among adults age 60 and over in 2021 (Table 1).

Challenges for an Aging World

The report covers cross-national comparisons on access to healthcare and social care, employment, retirement, volunteering, poverty, living arrangements and other age-related issues.

Among key findings:

Labor Force. Between 2012 and 2022, labor force participation among adults 65 and over fell in high‑income countries but rose in low- and middle-income countries.

Poverty . Among Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries in 2020, older adults in the United States (21.6%) and South Korea (40.5%) faced some of the highest poverty rates.

Caregiving. In many OECD countries, 3 out of 5 caregivers age 50 and over were women. Some high-income countries are beginning to compensate older caregivers to offset the health and financial stresses of caregiving.

Volunteering. More than 50% of the older population did volunteer work in the United Kingdom and New Zealand, compared to less than 10% in Ukraine, Guatemala and Cape Verde.

About the Report

An Aging World: 2025 is sponsored by the National Institute on Aging . It is the sixth report in the Aging World series which started in 1987. The report contains statistics from the Census Bureau’s International Database , the international family of Health and Retirement surveys , the Gateway to Global Aging , the World Bank and other data sources.

Mitali Sen is a branch chief and Rachel J. Bacon is a survey statistician and demographer at the Census Bureau.

Use of artificial intelligence (AI) by U.S. businesses has grown since December but varied by firm size and sector, according to the U.S. Census Bureau’s Business Trends and Outlook Survey (BTOS) .

The survey provides a biweekly, nationally representative view of AI implementation across the business landscape.

We reviewed the most recent six months of BTOS data collected from December 14, 2025 to May 3, 2026 to analyze trends in AI business usage.

The BTOS data (December 2025 to May 2026) show that overall AI usage hovered between 17% and 20% — and that between 20% and 23% of businesses expected to be using it in the next six months.

The BTOS captures two facets of AI adoption, asking the following questions (among others):

Whether the business used AI in the past two weeks.

Whether the business expects to use AI in the next six months.

Originally framed around AI use “in producing goods or services,” rather than to carry out simple tasks like drafting emails, the Census Bureau revised the wording last November to ask businesses whether they were using AI “in any business function.”

U.S. Business AI Use

The BTOS data (December 2025 to May 2026) show that overall AI usage hovered between 17% and 20% — and that between 20% and 23% of businesses expected to be using it in the next six months (Figure 1).

AI use by firm size shows similar trends (Figure 2).

For example, 37% of firms with at least 250 employees reported using AI in their business operations. In the data collection period ending May 3, 2026, 32% of firms with 100 to 249 employees said they used AI.

Between December 2025 and May 2026, AI use increased among firms with at least 20 employees but didn’t change significantly among firms with fewer than 20 employees. Less than 20% of firms with four or fewer employees reported using AI.

AI Trends Across Sectors

AI use remained relatively steady in many sectors over the last six months (Figure 3). The rate of expected use within these sectors also did not undergo any statistically significant changes:

As of May 3, 2026, the AI use rates in the Information (39.7%) and Finance and Insurance (33.9%) sectors were both higher than the national rate (19.8%) but neither reported significant shifts since December.

The expected usage rates in both sectors tells a similar story. About 42% of businesses in the Information sector and roughly 39% in Finance and Insurance expected to use AI in their business functions over the next six months, higher than the national average but not significantly different from the expected usage rate reported six months earlier.

In comparison, businesses in the Retail Trade sector reported current and expected usage lower than the national average: around 14% of businesses currently use AI, and about 17% expect to in the next six months.

Future Improvements to BTOS

The BTOS continues to evolve as new tools like AI emerge.

On November 17, 2025, BTOS began collecting data for its second AI supplement and revised the core AI use questions. This updated supplement expands on the original content by measuring AI use across 15 different business functions, including finance, human resources, customer service, marketing, information technology and research and development.

In addition, the supplement asks about AI-related operational changes, such as training, workflow adjustments and new technology investments.

The supplemental data also ask why a business is not using AI. Data for this experimental product can be found on this page and in this recently published working paper .

Adam Grundy is a supervisory statistician at the Census Bureau.

Cory Breaux is a survey statistician at the Census Bureau.

Dhanapati "Dhan" Khatiwoda is a mathematical statistician at the Census Bureau.

The 2026 Atlantic hurricane season that officially began June 1 has been mild — so far. There have been very few named storms in the Atlantic and the National Weather Service expects “below normal” hurricane activity.

But calm in the Atlantic could mean enhanced hurricane activity in the Pacific as El Niño warms seawater and lowers wind shear, a perfect storm for hurricane conditions.

Recently, Hurricane Lala ravaged parts of Hawaii, even though direct landfalls are rare in the state. Hurricane Lowell also brought more storm damage in the Pacific.

Coastal states face uncertainty during hurricane season but the Census Bureau has tools that can help communities prepare for the worst and plan for recovery from any disaster.

Hurricane damage is not exclusive to coastal areas. Take Buncombe County, North Carolina, located nearly 300 miles from the coast. Hurricane Helene devastated the county in 2024, leaving 43 dead and causing catastrophic flooding — proving once again that hurricane destruction does not stop at the shoreline.

In this story, we use Buncombe County to illustrate how Census Bureau tools can assist in planning and recovery.

Community Resilience Estimates

The Community Resilience Estimates (CRE) identify communities that may have difficulty withstanding and recovering from disasters because of certain factors like poverty, vehicle access and housing conditions.

These indicators are available for every state, county and neighborhood (census tract) in the United States and Puerto Rico.

The Community Resilience Estimates Viewer is an interactive tool that highlights the CRE and areas that may be vulnerable to disasters.

According to the map, for example,18.5% of people in Buncombe County may have difficulty recovering from natural disasters. This is statistically similar to the national estimate of 20.4% of the population.

Note: Select the image to go to the interactive data tool.

The CRE program continues to develop data products to assist with all stages of a disaster. To share feedback on current tools or suggest ideas for new disaster-related information, email the team at [email protected] .

CAREs: Assessment, Recovery and Evaluation

Hurricane Helene was one of the most devastating hurricanes in American history, responsible for at least 249 fatalities, more than 4 million power outages, and countless road and bridge collapses. The Census Bureau is currently prototyping tools to help gauge the full scale of its impact and in recovery efforts.

One resource is the Census Bureau’s Assessment, Recovery, and Evaluation datasets (CAREs ), which curates data from multiple federal sources, including the Census Bureau; Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA); Department of Energy (DOE); National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA); and Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS).

CAREs provides data users with relevant information about the population, disaster exposure and recovery all in one place.

Among the major findings : Nearly 1.5 million households registered for aid in counties with a disaster declaration.

This amounted to approximately 18 registrations for every 100 occupied households throughout the disaster area. In Buncombe County, that rate jumped to 86 registrations per 100 occupied households, underscoring the immense need for assistance within the county.

Census Business Builder

The Census Business Builder (CBB) is an interactive resource that provides key economic and demographic data down to the census tract level.

During declared disasters, this tool allows users to access detailed supply chain reports highlighting top imports, employment patterns, and potentially impacted products to help inform response and recovery efforts.

According to the CBB, some 826 U.S. employer establishments (those with at least one paid employee) closed and around 960 opened from March 2022 to March 2023 in Buncombe County.

Tracking future business shifts is important because it can help measure recovery efforts.

OnTheMap for Emergency Management

OnTheMap for Emergency Management is a tool that provides an easy-to-use mapping interface for viewing the potential impacts of natural disasters in the United States.

Maps, charts and reports include workforce, population and housing characteristics for hurricanes, floods, wildfires, winter storms and federal disaster declaration areas.

paragraphs: The 2026 Atlantic hurricane season that officially began June 1 has been mild — so far. There have been very few named storms in the Atlantic and the National Weather Service expects “below normal” hurricane activity.
But calm in the Atlantic could mean enhanced hurricane activity in the Pacific as El Niño warms seawater and lowers wind shear, a perfect storm for hurricane conditions.
Recently, Hurricane Lala ravaged parts of Hawaii, even though direct landfalls are rare in the state. Hurricane Lowell also brought more storm damage in the Pacific.
Coastal states face uncertainty during hurricane season but the Census Bureau has tools that can help communities prepare for the worst and plan for recovery from any disaster.

Hurricane damage is not exclusive to coastal areas. Take Buncombe County, North Carolina, located nearly 300 miles from the coast. Hurricane Helene devastated the county in 2024, leaving 43 dead and causing catastrophic flooding — proving once again that hurricane destruction does not stop at the shoreline.
In this story, we use Buncombe County to illustrate how Census Bureau tools can assist in planning and recovery.
Community Resilience Estimates

The Community Resilience Estimates (CRE) identify communities that may have difficulty withstanding and recovering from disasters because of certain factors like poverty, vehicle access and housing conditions.
These indicators are available for every state, county and neighborhood (census tract) in the United States and Puerto Rico.
The Community Resilience Estimates Viewer is an interactive tool that highlights the CRE and areas that may be vulnerable to disasters.

According to the map, for example,18.5% of people in Buncombe County may have difficulty recovering from natural disasters. This is statistically similar to the national estimate of 20.4% of the population.
Note: Select the image to go to the interactive data tool.

The CRE program continues to develop data products to assist with all stages of a disaster. To share feedback on current tools or suggest ideas for new disaster-related information, email the team at [email protected] .
CAREs: Assessment, Recovery and Evaluation

Hurricane Helene was one of the most devastating hurricanes in American history, responsible for at least 249 fatalities, more than 4 million power outages, and countless road and bridge collapses. The Census Bureau is currently prototyping tools to help gauge the full scale of its impact and in recovery efforts.

One resource is the Census Bureau’s Assessment, Recovery, and Evaluation datasets (CAREs ), which curates data from multiple federal sources, including the Census Bureau; Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA); Department of Energy (DOE); National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA); and Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS).
CAREs provides data users with relevant information about the population, disaster exposure and recovery all in one place.
Among the major findings : Nearly 1.5 million households registered for aid in counties with a disaster declaration.

This amounted to approximately 18 registrations for every 100 occupied households throughout the disaster area. In Buncombe County, that rate jumped to 86 registrations per 100 occupied households, underscoring the immense need for assistance within the county.
Census Business Builder
The Census Business Builder (CBB) is an interactive resource that provides key economic and demographic data down to the census tract level.

During declared disasters, this tool allows users to access detailed supply chain reports highlighting top imports, employment patterns, and potentially impacted products to help inform response and recovery efforts.
According to the CBB, some 826 U.S. employer establishments (those with at least one paid employee) closed and around 960 opened from March 2022 to March 2023 in Buncombe County.
Tracking future business shifts is important because it can help measure recovery efforts.

Overall Medicaid coverage declined between 2024 and 2025 for the second consecutive year, reflecting shifts in Medicaid policy, funding, eligibility and enrollment processes that began in 2020.

According to the U.S. Census Bureau’s 2021 to 2026 Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplements (CPS ASEC), Medicaid coverage rates rose from 2020 to 2021, didn’t change significantly from 2021 to 2023 and decreased from 2023 to 2025 (Figure 1).

Medicaid Changes

The Families First Coronavirus Response Act was passed and enacted in March 2020 in response to the COVID-19 pandemic. The measure required states to provide continuous coverage for those enrolled in Medicaid as a condition of receiving increased federal funding for the Medicaid program.

Congress later passed the American Rescue Plan Act of 2021, extending the continuous coverage mandate for the duration of the pandemic. The effects of these policies can be seen in the 0.9 percentage-point increase in Medicaid coverage between 2020 and 2021 and the sustained rates at this level through 2023 (Figure 1).

From 2020 to 2025, Medicaid coverage rates varied across regions . Rates were higher in the Northeast and the West than in the Midwest and the South.

Starting in April 2023, the mandated continuous coverage ended and additional Medicaid funding was gradually reduced and phased out. States began operating under standard eligibility and enrollment processes, which included terminations for individuals no longer eligible for Medicaid coverage.

This return to standard operations is commonly known as Medicaid unwinding . In general, states had 14 months to complete their eligibility and reenrollment processes. Most states, minus a few outliers, completed them by the end of 2024.

The effects of Medicaid unwinding can be seen in the decrease in Medicaid coverage in 2024 and 2025.

The CPS ASEC asks respondents if they had any health insurance coverage in the previous calendar year.

People are considered insured if covered by any type of health insurance, like Medicaid, at any point during the calendar year. An individual is considered uninsured if they had no health insurance at all during the calendar year.

As a result, individuals who lost Medicaid coverage at any point in 2024 due to the unwinding were still counted as having Medicaid coverage that year. Those losses did not show up until the following year — 2025 estimates captured in the 2026 CPS ASEC data released today .

Who Lost Medicaid Coverage?

Changes in Medicaid coverage rates from 2020 to 2025 for working-age adults (19 to 64) and children (under age 19) follow a similar pattern as changes in overall Medicaid coverage (Figure 2).

Children experienced a larger drop (2.0 percentage points) than working-age adults (1.1 percentage point) between 2023 and 2024, when the effects of Medicaid unwinding first took hold.

But unlike the total population and working-age adults — whose Medicaid coverage slipped 0.5 and 0.6 percentage points, respectively — children’s coverage didn’t change between 2024 and 2025. This was partly influenced by federal policies extending continuous eligibility and coverage protections for children .

Medicaid coverage of those 65 and older differed from that of other age groups. Their coverage didn’t change significantly from 2023 to 2024 and went up from 2024 to 2025.

Where Did Medicaid Coverage Change?

From 2020 to 2025, Medicaid coverage rates varied across regions . Rates were higher in the Northeast and the West than in the Midwest and the South (Figure 3).

Between 2020 and 2021, when continuous coverage was in effect, Medicaid coverage rates increased in the Northeast and the Midwest but did not significantly change for people in the South and the West.

From 2023 to 2024, when the impact of Medicaid unwinding became apparent, Medicaid coverage declined in the Northeast, South and West and did not significantly change in the Midwest. Between 2024 and 2025, Medicaid coverage decreased in the South by 0.6 percentage points, the lowest rate among all regions in 2025 (14.9%).

It is important to note that some states expanded Medicaid eligibility (expansion states) between 2020 and 2025, in accordance with the Affordable Care Act that gave states the option to expand Medicaid eligibility to people who fell under a particular poverty threshold.

As of January 1, 2025, all states in the Northeast, all but one in the West, 10 out of 12 states in the Midwest and 10 out of 17 states in the South had adopted expansion.

The 10 states that had not expanded Medicaid eligibility (nonexpansion states) as of January 1, 2025, were Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Kansas, Mississippi, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, Wisconsin, and Wyoming. Of these, seven are in the South, two in the Midwest, and one in the West.
